title: Priorization of Exome Data with Image Analysis Aachen
summary:
In many genetic disorders, disease-specific features reflected in image data, such as photographs of the face, X-rays of bones, or images of the back of the eye in retinal diseases, provide a clue to the disease and thus to the possible underlying genetic cause. A good example of this is Down syndrome. Many people immediately recognize an affected person by special facial features, because people with Down syndrome often resemble each other in these features. Specialized medical staff can recognize many more and rarer disorders by specific external features (e.g., of the eyes, ears, or bones). However, a prerequisite for this is appropriate and sufficient experience with the individual clinical pictures. But it is precisely this experience that is often lacking in the case of rare diseases.
Modern computer-aided methods of image analysis can learn to recognize such peculiarities and thus reliably calculate similarities to individuals with an already confirmed diagnosis. Studies have already shown that the diagnosis rate is significantly increased by combining clinical examination with the aid of computerized image analysis.  Like medical professionals, however, the computer system must first learn the characteristics of the diseases in order to recognize them. Various programs, such as GestaltMatcher, use artificial intelligence (AI) that can recognize not only diseases it has already learned about, but also diseases it is not yet familiar with. It also requires significantly fewer images of affected individuals than comparable systems to make the correct diagnosis. Such computational methods can provide medical professionals with a clue to a genetic disorder and assist in selecting a particular molecular test. AI can also be used to interpret the results of molecular genetic testing.
In our research study PEDIA AC, we aim to investigate and improve the quality of currently available image analysis methods (e.g. GestaltMatcher). For this purpose, we would like to enroll about 150 patients per year in this study.
conditions: Patients with phenotypic abnormalities reflected in imaging data, such as facial dysmorphic signs, and with suspected rare underlying genetic disease as the cause should be included.

interventions.name:

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with phenotypic abnormalities reflected in imaging data, such as facial dysmorphic signs, and with suspected rare underlying genetic disease as the cause will be included.
Exclusion criteria:
If there are no phenotypic abnormalities or no patient consent, inclusion in the study is not possible.
